title: Middleware and the Request Pipeline
summary: Learn what middleware is, why its order matters, and how to write your own for request ids, timing, and errors.
intro: Every request Roombook answers needs the same chores done around it. It needs an id, so you can find it in the logs. It needs a log line saying how long it took, security headers, a CORS check for the web app, its JSON body read, and a clean answer when something crashes. Writing those into every handler would copy the same lines dozens of times, and the one handler that forgets them becomes the hole. **Middleware** is how a server does each chore once, for every request. This lesson explains what middleware is and why its order matters. Then you write your own for request ids and timing, add one place that turns every crash into a clean answer, and meet the filters, interceptors, and advice Spring gives you.

steps.title: What middleware is

examples.title: A filter that never passes the request on
examples.prompt: With the forgetful filter registered, ask for the rooms.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 
X-Request-Id: d44e875d-4a6c-4696-823e-e9969037fc2b
Content-Length: 0
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:45 GMT
examples.explanation: The status says `200`, and it's a lie. The filter logged the request and returned without calling `chain.doFilter`, so the controller never ran. Nothing set a status or wrote a body, and Tomcat finished the response the only way it could: the default status, 200, with `Content-Length: 0`. The `X-Request-Id` header is there because the request id filter from part 3 runs before this one. A client sees an empty success, which is worse than an error, since nothing looks wrong. When a Spring endpoint answers an empty 200, look for a filter with a branch that returns without calling the chain.

steps.title: Order matters
steps.body:
Middleware runs in the order you set up, and each one can see what earlier ones did, or stop the request before later ones see it. So the order is part of the design. Get it wrong and the bugs are confusing: log lines without request ids, a crash that skips the error handler, a login check that runs after the expensive work it was meant to prevent, or a handler that finds no body.

## Roombook's order

Here is the order Roombook uses, from the outside in, and why each piece sits where it does:

1. **Request id** comes first, so everything after it, logging included, can use the id.
2. **Logging and timing** come next. They wrap as much of the work as possible, so the time they report is close to what the client waited, and so every answer gets a log line, even an early refusal.
3. **Security headers** come early, so they're on every response, error answers and early refusals included.
4. **CORS** comes before anything that might refuse the request. A browser's **preflight**, the OPTIONS request it sends first to ask whether a cross-site call is allowed, has to get its answer even though it carries no login and no body.
5. **Body parsing** turns the JSON text into data, with a size limit, before any handler needs it.
6. **Rate limiting**, in the Redis lesson, comes before authentication, so a flood of password guesses is turned away before each one costs a password check.
7. **Authentication**, in the authentication lesson, works out who is calling before any handler decides what they may do.
8. The **router** picks a handler from the method and the path, and the **handler** does the work.
9. **Error handling** catches whatever went wrong anywhere above, so every failure becomes a clean response.

## The chain in Spring

A request to a Spring app crosses two worlds. First come the **filters**, which belong to Tomcat and the Servlet standard, and run before Spring MVC has looked at the request at all. Then the last filter hands the request to the DispatcherServlet, Spring MVC's front door from the routes lesson. It finds the controller method for the path, runs any **interceptors** registered for it, converts the JSON body into the method's parameter, and calls the method. When the method throws an exception, the DispatcherServlet hands it to your **controller advice**, a class marked `@RestControllerAdvice` that turns exceptions into responses.

```diagram middleware-chain
A request's path through Spring. Spring Security's filters arrive in the authentication lesson.
```

Filters run in the order of their `@Order` value, lowest number first. `Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE`, the lowest number there is, puts Roombook's request id filter outside every other filter, Spring Boot's own included, so every log line carries the id:

```java sketch
@Component
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    ...
}
```

A filter with no `@Order` gets the lowest precedence, and runs after every ordered one. In the authentication lesson, Spring Security adds its whole chain as one filter at order -100, so a filter that must see every request, even ones security refuses, needs a number below that.

Two items on the list above happen inside the DispatcherServlet in Spring, not in filters. Body parsing happens when it converts the body into your `@RequestBody` parameter, right before your method runs. CORS is checked once it has found the handler, at least until the security lesson moves CORS into Spring Security's chain.

## Global, path, and handler scope

- **Global**: a filter bean runs for every request. A `FilterRegistrationBean` can limit a filter to some URL patterns, and set its order in code instead of with `@Order`.
- **Path**: an interceptor is registered with path patterns, like `registry.addInterceptor(timing).addPathPatterns("/v1/**")`.
- **Handler**: an interceptor's `preHandle` receives the controller method that was chosen, so it can act on annotations it finds on that method. The permissions lesson guards single methods with an annotation too, `@PreAuthorize`, though Spring Security checks it through a proxy, which the lesson on layers previews.

Part 5 shows an interceptor in full.

examples.title: Filters, then the interceptor, then the controller
examples.prompt: Two filter beans log before and after `chain.doFilter`, with orders 1 and 2. The interceptor from part 5 logs which controller method was picked, and the controller logs `controller`. Ask for the rooms once, and read the server's terminal.
examples.output:
23:50:43.261 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] demo - first filter: before
23:50:43.261 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] demo - second filter: before
23:50:43.266 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] d.h.r.c.HandlerTimingInterceptor - handled by RoomController.list
23:50:43.269 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] demo - controller
23:50:43.287 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] demo - second filter: after
23:50:43.288 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] demo - first filter: after
23:50:43.288 INFO  [079562aa-09c6-4348-8946-915f8545a07b] d.h.r.c.RequestIdFilter - GET /v1/rooms 200 26.8ms
examples.explanation: Each line carries the request id in brackets, thanks to the request id filter, which has the highest precedence and so wraps everything. The filter with order 1 ran first and finished last, and order 2 sat inside it, the onion from part 1. Only after both filters had passed the request on did the DispatcherServlet pick `RoomController.list`, which the interceptor logged, and call it. Then the response unwound through the filters in reverse, and the request id filter wrote the timing line last. Filters can't know which controller will run, since Spring hasn't chosen yet when they run. Interceptors can.

steps.title: Your own middleware: request ids and timing

examples.title: An id made, and an id kept
examples.prompt: Ask for the rooms twice: once with no id, and once sending your own. `grep` keeps only the id header from each response.
examples.code: curl -si localhost:8080/v1/rooms | grep -i "^x-request-id"; curl -si -H "X-Request-Id: demo-42" localhost:8080/v1/rooms | grep -i "^x-request-id"
examples.explanation: The first request had no `X-Request-Id`, so the filter made a UUID and sent it back. The second sent `demo-42`, which passes the check, so the server kept it, and the log lines above show these same ids in brackets. A proxy that already gives each request an id keeps it all the way through, and a client that sends its own can quote it to support without reading any header. Send an id with a space in it, and you get a fresh UUID instead.

examples.title: A write in read-only mode
examples.prompt: Start the server with `--roombook.read-only=true` after the run command, and try to create a booking.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 503 
X-Request-Id: e4e95c53-36fb-48cc-b759-00f46a78482d
Retry-After: 600
Content-Type: application/json;charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 62
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:48 GMT
Connection: close

{"status":503,"title":"Roombook is read-only for maintenance"}
examples.explanation: The middleware answered by itself: `503 Service Unavailable` with `Retry-After: 600`, ten minutes, and the booking route never ran. A well-behaved client waits that long and tries again, instead of hammering a server that's busy. The request still has an `X-Request-Id`, because the request id layer sits outside the read-only one, so even this refusal can be found in the logs. A `GET` goes through as usual, since reading changes nothing. The error body is a first draft: the next lesson replaces it with the standard error format every Roombook error uses.

steps.title: Catching errors in one place

examples.title: A path that doesn't exist, and a crash
examples.prompt: Ask for a path no controller has, then for a test endpoint that throws `IllegalStateException("connection to the database was lost")`.
examples.output:
{"detail":"No static resource v1/nope.","status":404,"title":"Not Found"}
HTTP/1.1 500 
X-Request-Id: 4583805e-1bb3-4c7b-9d87-d2a36a9c1847
Vary: Origin
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Method
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:40 GMT
Connection: close

{"requestId":"4583805e-1bb3-4c7b-9d87-d2a36a9c1847","status":500,"title":"Internal Server Error"}
examples.explanation: The first answer came from `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`: no controller matched, Spring threw `NoResourceFoundException`, and the base class answered 404 in a JSON shape called a `ProblemDetail`, which the next lesson builds on. Its `detail` mentions a static resource because Spring's last try, when no controller matches, is to look for a file to serve. The second answer came from your handler: a generic 500 with the request id, and nothing about the database. The server's terminal has the rest, an `ERROR` line with the same id in brackets, the exception, and its stack trace. Tomcat writes no reason phrase after the status code, so the status line is just `HTTP/1.1 500`, which is allowed, since clients only read the number.

steps.title: Interceptors and Spring's built-in filters

examples.title: A CORS preflight
examples.prompt: Act like the browser running Roombook's web app on `localhost:5173`: send the OPTIONS preflight it sends before a POST with a JSON body.
examples.code: curl -si -X OPTIONS localhost:8080/v1/bookings -H "Origin: http://localhost:5173" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type"
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 
X-Request-Id: b18af4bc-3c8c-43e6-a6f3-4995b6080bb1
Vary: Origin
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Method
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type
Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Request-Id, Location, ETag
Access-Control-Max-Age: 1800
Allow: GET, HEAD, PATCH, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS
Content-Length: 0
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:50:40 GMT
examples.explanation: The DispatcherServlet found that `POST /v1/bookings` exists, saw a preflight from an allowed origin, and answered it from the rules in `addCorsMappings`, without calling the controller. `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` names the web app's origin, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` lists what was configured, and `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` lets the web app's JavaScript read `X-Request-Id` and `Location` from real responses, which browsers hide otherwise. `Access-Control-Max-Age: 1800` lets the browser reuse this answer for half an hour. `X-Request-Id` is there because the filter ran first, as it does for every request. The next lesson checks everything a request carries, and gives every error one format.

recap:
- Middleware is code that runs around every handler, for jobs that cut across all routes, like ids, logs, headers, and errors.
- The pipeline is an onion: each layer works on the way in, calls the rest, and works again on the way out.
- A middleware can read the request, add to it, answer early, or act on the response, and forgetting to pass the request on is a classic bug.
- Order is design: request id and logging outermost, CORS before anything that refuses, body parsing before handlers, errors at the edge.
- A request id, kept from X-Request-Id when it's safe or made fresh, ties a request's log lines together and goes back to the client.
- Per-request values live in the MDC, never in globals, since one server works on many requests at once.
- One error handler logs the details and answers a generic 500 with the request id, and unknown paths get a JSON 404.
- Scope middleware to where it's needed: the whole app, a group of routes, or one route.
